story1014:
The Ojibwe creation story tells how Nanabozho, the son of Epingishmook (the West Wind) and a human mother, was born with great spiritual powers. After his mother died, he was raised by his grandmother, who taught him the ways of the spirit world.

Nanabozho grew into a powerful being — part human, part spirit. He could transform into any animal, command the wind, and speak with the dead. He was a trickster and a teacher, a hero and a fool.

When the great flood came — caused by Nanabozho's own anger at the underwater serpents who killed his twin brother — he survived by floating on a log with the animals. The world was destroyed, and Nanabozho was filled with remorse.

From the mud brought up by the muskrat, Nanabozho created Turtle Island — the North American continent. He shaped the rivers and mountains, the forests and plains. He brought the animals back from the dead and placed them in the new world.

But the creation was imperfect. Nanabozho was not a perfect creator. He made mistakes — the mosquito was an accident, the poison ivy was a miscalculation, the coyote was a joke. The world was beautiful but flawed, just like its creator.

The Ojibwe tell this story to teach that creation is not a finished act but an ongoing process. The world is still being made, still being shaped by the forces that Nanabozho set in motion. And Nanabozho himself is still here — walking the earth, tricking the unwary, teaching the wise.
story1015:
A newly married couple had a baby boy who seemed normal until one day, while still in his cradleboard, he spoke to his parents saying he would visit the Sky Spirit. That night, the baby vanished from his cradleboard.

His parents searched everywhere — in the lodge, in the village, along the river, in the forest. They called his name until their voices were hoarse. They wept until they had no tears left. But the baby was gone.

Years passed. The boy returned as a young man, tall and strong, his face marked with the signs of the sky world. He told his parents of his journey — of the Sky Spirit's lodge, of the paths between the stars, of the beings that live in the spaces between worlds.

The people were amazed. They gathered to hear his stories, to learn what the sky world was like. The young man spoke of the Sky Spirit's wisdom, of the rules that govern the universe, of the connection between the earth and the heavens.

But he also warned them: the Windigo was coming. The great cannibal spirit of the north, with its heart of ice and its endless hunger, was moving south. The people must prepare.

The story teaches that knowledge comes from unexpected sources, and that even the youngest among us can carry the wisdom of the spirits. The baby who went to the sky returned with the knowledge that would save his people.
story1016:
A Windigo as tall as a white pine tree approached a village, its approach signaled by a kettle swinging over the fire and trees cracking from the bitter cold. The villagers were terrified, but a wise old grandmother knew what had to be done.

She told the people to heat a great kettle of water and to fill it with hot stones until the water was boiling. Then she told the youngest girl in the village — a girl of twelve winters — to carry the kettle to the Windigo.

The girl was afraid but obedient. She took the kettle in her small hands and walked toward the Windigo. The cold was terrible — her breath froze in the air, her fingers burned with frost, her feet left bloody prints in the snow.

But she kept walking. She walked until she stood before the Windigo, its height blocking out the sky, its breath a blizzard of ice and snow. She lifted the kettle and poured the boiling water into the Windigo's open mouth.

The water melted the Windigo's ice heart. It screamed — a sound like a mountain cracking — and fell. Its body shattered into a thousand pieces, and from those pieces, the first evergreen trees grew.

The girl was carried back to the village by the people, who praised her courage. She had faced the most terrifying creature in the world and defeated it with nothing but a kettle of hot water and the courage of her convictions.

The story teaches that the smallest and most vulnerable can defeat the greatest evil, and that courage is not the absence of fear but the decision to act despite it.
